title: Report on Studying Abroad at Duke University
paragraphs: I was allowed to study abroad at Duke University as an exchange student for about two months. I would like to report on my life abroad, which I got through with the support of many people both before and after the clerkship began. 1. Consultative Cardiology On the first day of the clerkship, after receiving an orientation at 8 a.m. from the assistant professor, Dr. Waugh, I was told to first join the rounds, was introduced to the attending, and joined the rounds without really understanding what was going on. It started with figuring out what the composition of this team was and what its duties were. Fortunately, a second-year Duke student had been rotating for two weeks already, so I was able to get through the first week somehow by asking him many things. The team I belonged to was called the Teaching Service. This team was divided into two types, a ward team and a consult team. Students were assigned to the consult team, and the students' job was, before the fellow went to a consult, to first take the patient's information, physical findings, test findings and so on, summarise them, think up my own assessment and plan, present it to the fellow, decide the policy from then on with the attending, and follow up together. In the first week, both morning and afternoon I basically accompanied the attending on rounds, but when the fellow went to see a consult patient, I was called and saw the patient together with him. From the second week, as I had got used to the English, I gradually came to be entrusted with things, going to see consult patients together with the Duke student or by myself. From the third week the Duke student was gone, so I acted together with the fellow. Whenever we saw any patient, he always asked for my opinion and gave me appropriate feedback. If I said what I wanted to do, they would respond accordingly, so I think the cardiology rotation was very fulfilling for getting used to America and studying. Also, on Tuesday and Wednesday mornings from 7 a.m., there was a physical examination lecture by Dr. Waugh for about two hours, with training in interpreting chest palpation and auscultation using simulators. This too was very educational. 2. Pulmonary Medicine In the pulmonary rotation too, I was assigned to the consult team. Here too, the students' role was the same as in cardiology. By the pulmonary rotation I had also got used to English, and on the whole I was entrusted with about one consult a day. (As a result, the number of patients I was in charge of kept increasing, and I made rounds from early in the morning.) Of course, in the end the attending also writes the treatment policy, but since the present illness, findings and A/P I wrote were also used, I felt both fear of that responsibility and a sense of fulfilment, and I naturally had more opportunities to meet patients and talk with them and to search the literature on their diseases. The fellow who was in charge of me always gave appropriate feedback on my presentations. Not only differential diagnoses I had not thought of, but also the importance of presentations, that is, how to convey logically the differential diagnoses I was considering, how to construct the present illness for that purpose, how to summarise in the way that conveys most effectively, how to convey my thoughts through a presentation and get others to agree, he taught me carefully and took his time. As I repeated this every day, I think I improved considerably. Although I was attached to pulmonary, being able to polish the general presentation skills that I had been poor at is one of the major gains for me. What impressed me most overall was the attitude of American doctors toward clinical education. At Duke University, many conferences were held every day in the morning, at noon and in the evening. Questions and opinions flew back and forth, and heated discussions unfolded. The atmosphere of improving one another in that way is very stimulating. Scenes of American doctors listening well to the thoughts of students and junior doctors and discussing with them could be seen everywhere. Pharmacists and nurses also joined in, and it was very impressive how the discussion, starting from patients' treatment policy, developed into EBM and the latest clinical trials. I think it was a valuable experience in which I learned a great deal by receiving this kind of American-style education. The two months passed in the blink of an eye, but they became a very fulfilling period. In these two months I met various people and was able to think deeply about my own future and about Japanese medical care, and I think my own way of thinking about medicine has broadened considerably. I would like to thank Dr. 粕谷 and 長縄-san of the International Exchange Office of Nagoya University, 西尾-san of the academic affairs office, Dr. 坂本 of YLP, Dean Dr. 濱口, the people at Duke University, 黒田-kun who studied abroad with me, all the exchange students of 2008, and everyone else who helped me, who gave me this valuable and wonderful opportunity. Thank you very much.
